title: Feedback on My Intro / Ship Sinking Sequence?
author: SocialContractGuy
selftext:
I’m developing a survival adventure game called [Washed Ashore](https://thesocialcontractgame.com/). I’m trying to strike a balance between an engaging opening that doesn’t drag on but gives players enough reason to care about the characters and keep playing.  
A little background: I’m not a programmer. I’ve been building this using Claude Code for programming, Meshy for 3D models, and some Kenney assets. I handle the story, game design, creative direction, and playtesting, while AI handles the technical implementation. It’s been a very iterative process.  
I’d love some honest feedback on the opening sequence

Does it hold your attention?  
Is the pacing too slow or too fast?  
Does it make you curious about what happens next?  
What would you change?  
Still very much a work in progress!

comments.author: lucianw
comments.body:
Sorry to be a downer. The way I see it, I love to put my time into something that will be rewarding. That will be a creative or interesting story, engaging characters, clever gameplay mechanics. I'm unable to judge that in the first five minutes, so I have to use proxies, e.g. "the creator obviously put their creative talent to work in this thing I can observe in the first minute or two so I trust enough that they've got a similar level of talent in the aspects that are ultimately rewarding".

In this case the animations were honestly  bad. I never like idle animations in general, but these combined idle animations with slow delivery and characters that were uncanny and didn't look like they were created with soul. The sea background also felt a bit like a kind of featureless limbo.

(also I was a bit irritated that my two-letter name wasn't accepted! Ty. Jo. Ed.)

I suspect that your strengths might be in storybuilding and writing. If so, you're locking them away behind lackluster animations. What if you walked up to someone and it just presented the entire text of what they have to say so my brain could enter "text interaction" mode rather than aiming to be a real-time conversation? That way I wouldn't be looking at the animations...

replies.author: SocialContractGuy
replies.body: Gotcha good to know. I guess my fear was a wall of text would scare some players away

comments.author: Gigaslavx
comments.body:
https://i.redd.it/mq30slosns3i1.png

models are a bit weird overall the style is interesting. personally you want to watch diminishing returns sometimes its better to go simpler and be upfront about it, somewhat of a player contract where the player is willing to compromise. in this case its like you promise a lot and the expectations are higher. i do like the general background graphics despite being simple it works relatively well

replies.author: SocialContractGuy
replies.body: Thanks for the insight. I have def made a ton of progress with what I think is a great plot but if the characters are too uncanny and weird. I may have to go back to square one

comments.author: DrinkingAtQuarks
comments.body:
Couple of notes: 

You explain the set up of why you're on the boat and where you're going, which removes all mystery. Without mystery why would a player want to continue?

First interaction, chat with an old man on the bow of a ship. The mesh of the old man is generic and neither invites analysis nor delights visually. His mesh clips through the gunwhale of the boat. My head (the camera) stays locked in space while the boat moves under me. This lack of finesse is instantly off putting.

Your opening set up is essentially the same as Skyrim. If you want to learn and improve watch the intro of Skyrim a few times and take some notes about what makes it effective and how it differs from your attempt. Good luck 👍

replies.author: SocialContractGuy
replies.body: Interesting perspective. Out of curiosity what do you think is the core mystery of the game?

replies.author: SocialContractGuy
replies.body: Did you make it to the island?
